prompt:
A 75-year-old man was recently diagnosed with myositis and is on high-dose steroids, methotrexate, and IVIG, with plans for a prolonged steroid taper. His QuantiFERON test was positive. He has no active symptoms of TB and has a recently normal chest x-ray. On examination, he has mild bilateral pedal edema. How should his latent TB be treated?

Provide a stepwise therapeutic management plan including medications, counseling, and follow-up.

rubric_items.text: Initiate latent tuberculosis treatment promptly during ongoing immunosuppression after active TB has been excluded.
Perform a symptom screen for active tuberculosis before starting latent TB therapy.
Review the recent chest radiograph for findings suggesting prior or active tuberculosis.
Obtain a detailed history of prior TB exposure, testing, and treatment.
Obtain baseline AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin before starting therapy.
Obtain a baseline complete blood count.
Assess baseline renal function before treatment.
Obtain HIV screening.
Obtain hepatitis B screening.
Review all current medications for interactions with isoniazid and rifamycins before selecting a regimen.

Select a guideline-recommended LTBI regimen after reviewing interactions: a short-course rifamycin regimen (e.g. 3 months of weekly isoniazid-rifapentine or 4 months of daily rifampin) when interactions can be safely managed, or daily isoniazid for 6–9 months when rifamycins are unsuitable; include pyridoxine 25–50 mg daily with any isoniazid-containing regimen.
Counsel the patient to stop therapy and seek care if symptoms of hepatotoxicity develop.
Repeat hepatic function testing within 2–4 weeks after treatment begins.
Schedule clinical follow-up within 2–4 weeks to assess tolerance and adherence.
Counsel the patient to seek prompt evaluation if symptoms of active tuberculosis develop.
Counsel the patient to avoid alcohol during latent TB treatment.
Counsel the patient regarding the importance of completing the full treatment course.
Refer to an infectious diseases specialist or TB clinic for co-management.
Discuss latent TB regimen options and obtain informed consent.
Document treatment completion and provide the patient with written treatment records.
Coordinate treatment timing with rheumatology before any further intensification of immunosuppression.
Collect sputum for AFB smear and mycobacterial culture despite the absence of symptoms and a normal chest radiograph.
Withhold or indefinitely defer indicated latent TB treatment without a valid clinical reason, including solely because the chest radiograph is normal.
Initiate empiric four-drug RIPE therapy without evidence of active tuberculosis.
Prescribe isoniazid without pyridoxine supplementation.
Prescribe a rifampin-based regimen without a plan to manage clinically significant drug interactions, particularly reduced systemic corticosteroid exposure.
Repeat QuantiFERON testing or perform a tuberculin skin test solely to confirm the positive result.
Order chest CT solely for latent TB evaluation in this asymptomatic patient with a normal chest radiograph.
Perform bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage in this asymptomatic patient with a normal chest radiograph.
Discontinue methotrexate or corticosteroid therapy solely to permit latent TB treatment.
Abruptly stop high-dose corticosteroids to reduce TB reactivation risk.
Prescribe fluoroquinolone monotherapy for presumed drug-susceptible latent TB without an MDR/RR-TB exposure indication or other specialist-directed justification.
Use a pyrazinamide-containing regimen for latent tuberculosis.
Start hepatotoxic latent TB therapy without obtaining baseline liver tests.
Administer BCG vaccine as treatment for latent tuberculosis.
Prescribe streptomycin for latent tuberculosis.
Arrange at least monthly clinical follow-up through treatment completion, with ongoing liver-test monitoring given concurrent methotrexate and elevated hepatotoxicity risk.
